metadata.title: Investigating the relationship between teacher efficacy, job satisfaction, and digital resource utilization in assessment practices: Insights from PISA 2018 and 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data (teacher-level responses) merged across two teacher questionnaire files and analyzed across 24 countries. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex-sampling weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and does not describe replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the paper applies SEM and regularized linear regression as “machine learning” components, it does not document whether survey-weighted estimation was used; this omission limits the ability to assess representativeness under PISA’s clustered school sampling. The analytic sample is restricted by country inclusion (excluding low-income countries) and by the availability of the specified questionnaire items for the five constructs (TE, JS, AP, UIT, UDT), but the exact missing-data exclusion/imputation rule is not reported.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the reported ML/regularized regression and SEM are latent constructs derived from teacher questionnaire Likert-type items (teacher efficacy, job satisfaction, assessment practices, and technology-use frequencies), not cognitive achievement scores with PISA Plausible Values. As a result, PV handling is not applicable to the modeled outcomes. The manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) for the questionnaire items used to form the constructs, which is a reporting gap because missingness can affect construct scores and regression/SEM estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 (post-pandemic) teacher questionnaire data, merged from two teacher questionnaire files (CY07_MSU_TCH_QQQ and CY08MSP_TCH_QQQ) using common variables. Countries were restricted to 24 economies categorized by World Bank income classification for 2022–2023, explicitly excluding low-income countries due to data unavailability. The constructs TE, JS, AP, UIT, and UDT were operationalized from 31 teacher-questionnaire items across five constructs; the analysis therefore relies on respondents with the relevant item responses for these constructs, but the exact missing-item handling/exclusion rule is not reported.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 Teacher Questionnaire (post-pandemic), 24 countries
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regularized regression (item-wise effects) — MSE: 0.28; scaled MSE: 0.95; RMSE: 0.52; MAE/MAD: 0.42; MAPE: 16.50%; R²: 0.27. SEM fit: NFI/RFI/IFI/TLI/CFI = 0.86–0.88; RMSEA = 0.06. SEM path: TE → AP (Beta = 0.37); UIT → AP (Beta = 0.37); UDT → AP (Beta = 0.35); JS → AP (Beta = 0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data across 24 countries, the study leveraged teacher efficacy, job satisfaction, and technology-use measures (UIT/UDT) to predict assessment practices, finding that teacher efficacy and both technology-use constructs had positive associations with assessment practices while job satisfaction had a near-zero direct effect (SEM Beta = 0.37/0.37/0.35 vs. Beta = 0.01). This indicates that strengthening teacher efficacy and supporting teachers’ digital tool integration may be more actionable for improving assessment practices than focusing solely on job satisfaction, though the study’s predictive performance is moderate (R² = 0.27) and causal claims cannot be inferred from cross-sectional questionnaire data.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 Teacher Questionnaire (post-pandemic), 24 countries
main_findings.target_variable: Use of digital learning & communication tools (UDT)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regularized regression (item-wise effects) — MSE: 0.16; scaled MSE: 0.52; RMSE: 0.40; MAE/MAD: 0.31; MAPE: 16.74%; R²: 0.55. SEM fit: NFI/RFI/IFI/TLI/CFI = 0.86–0.88; RMSEA = 0.06. SEM paths: JS → UDT (Beta = 0.01); TE → UDT (Beta = 0.88); UIT → UDT (Beta = 0.88).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data across 24 countries, the study leveraged teacher efficacy, job satisfaction, and instructional technology use (UIT) to predict use of digital learning and communication tools (UDT), finding that teacher efficacy strongly predicted UDT (SEM Beta = 0.88) while job satisfaction had essentially no direct effect (SEM Beta = 0.01). This indicates that policies aiming to build teacher efficacy (e.g., training that produces mastery experiences) are likely to be more effective for increasing digital communication tool adoption than job-satisfaction initiatives alone, while acknowledging that the model’s predictive fit is better for UDT than for UIT (R² = 0.55) and that survey-weighting and missing-data handling are not documented.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 Teacher Questionnaire (post-pandemic), 24 countries
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regularized regression (item-wise effects) — MSE: 0.35; scaled MSE: 1.37; RMSE: 0.59; MAE/MAD: 0.46; MAPE: 29.26%; R²: 0.10. SEM fit: NFI/RFI/IFI/TLI/CFI = 0.86–0.88; RMSEA = 0.06. SEM paths: JS → UIT (Beta = −0.32); TE → UIT (Beta = 0.37); UIT/UDT → AP (reported separately).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data across 24 countries, the study leveraged teacher efficacy, job satisfaction, and digital tool use to predict use of instructional technology tools (UIT), finding that job satisfaction had a negative association with UIT (SEM Beta = −0.32) and that teacher efficacy’s effect on UIT was weaker than on UDT (SEM Beta = 0.37), with low explanatory power for UIT (R² = 0.10). This indicates that increasing teachers’ efficacy may not be sufficient to raise instructional-tool use in the same way as digital communication tools, and that job-satisfaction-related mechanisms (e.g., technostress or implementation quality) may require targeted mitigation for instructional technology adoption.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Teacher Questionnaire (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 Teacher Questionnaire (post-pandemic), 24 countries
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regularized regression (item-wise effects) — MSE: 0.30; scaled MSE: 1.23; RMSE: 0.54; MAE/MAD: 0.45; MAPE: 15.04%; R²: 0.15. SEM fit: NFI/RFI/IFI/TLI/CFI = 0.86–0.88; RMSEA = 0.06. SEM path: JS → TE (Beta = 0.40).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire data across 24 countries, the study leveraged job satisfaction to predict teacher efficacy, finding a positive association (SEM Beta = 0.40) and modest predictive fit (R² = 0.15). This indicates that improving aspects of teachers’ job satisfaction and workplace support may help build teacher efficacy, which in turn supports technology adoption and assessment practices, though the study’s model fit for TE is limited and the analysis does not document how missing questionnaire responses were handled.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PISA 2018 (pre-pandemic) and PISA 2022 (post-pandemic) teacher questionnaire data for 128,866 teachers across 24 countries (excluding low-income economies). It models five constructs—teacher efficacy (TE), job satisfaction (JS), assessment practices (AP), use of instructional technology tools (UIT), and use of digital learning/communication tools (UDT)—using SEM and a regularized regression “machine learning” component with item-wise effects. Predictive performance is strongest for UDT (R² = 0.55; RMSE = 0.40; MAPE = 16.74%) and weakest for UIT (R² = 0.10; RMSE = 0.59; MAPE = 29.26%), while AP shows moderate fit (R² = 0.27; RMSE = 0.52). SEM indicates TE strongly predicts UDT (Beta = 0.88) and AP (Beta = 0.37), whereas JS has a strong effect on TE (Beta = 0.40) but minimal direct effect on AP (Beta = 0.01) and a negative association with UIT (Beta = −0.32). Limitations include unreported missing-data handling and unclear use of PISA sampling weights, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
